Let $A$ and $B$ be two independent events from a sample space.

If $P(A)=p$, $P(B)=p^2$, then which of the following is an expression for $P\left(\overline{A}\cup B\right)$?

Using the addition rule, then independence of $A$ and $B$ (so $\overline{A}$ and $B$ are independent):
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(\overline{A}\cup B\right)&=P\left(\overline{A}\right)+P(B)-P\left(\overline{A}\cap B\right) \\ &=P\left(\overline{A}\right)+P(B)-P\left(\overline{A}\right)P(B) \\ &=(1-p)+p^2-(1-p)p^2 \\ &=1-p+p^2-p^2+p^3 \\ &=1-p+p^3 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
$$\text{Probability (player misses in 1 attempt)}=1-0.15=0.85$$
$$\text{Probability (player misses in both attempts)}=(0.85)^2=0.7225$$

The player scores at least one goal unless every one of the $n$ attempts misses:
$$P(\text{at least one goal})=1-(0.85)^n$$
We need
$$\begin{aligned} 1-(0.85)^n &> 0.8\\ (0.85)^n &< 0.2\end{aligned}$$
Taking logs (and dividing by $\ln(0.85)<0$ reverses the inequality):
$$\begin{aligned} n\ln(0.85) &< \ln(0.2)\\ n &> \dfrac{\ln(0.2)}{\ln(0.85)}\\ &\approx 9.90\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Provides the correct inequality, $(0.85)^n<0.2$, or equivalent merit

Two independent events $A$ and $B$ are given such that $P(A)=m$ and $P(B)=m+0.4$.

It is known that $P(A\cap B)=0.21$.

What is the value of $P(A\cup B)$?

$A$ and $B$ are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
$$\begin{aligned} m(m+0.4)&=0.21\\ m^2+0.4m-0.21&=0\\ (m+0.7)(m-0.3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
A probability cannot be negative, so $m=0.3$, giving $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.7$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\ &=0.3+0.7-0.21\\ &=0.79 \end{aligned}$$

A die is loaded such that in a roll of a single die the chance of rolling a 1 is $\dfrac{x}{4}$, the chance of rolling a 2 is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and the chance of rolling a 6 is $\dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)$. The chance of rolling the other numbers (3,4 or 5) remain one in 6.

Two such dice are rolled together and the numbers on the uppermost faces are added to obtain a total score for the roll.

The probability of the total score of the two dice being 7 can be expressed as $y=f(x)$

Find the probability of rolling a 1 in a single roll of a die if the probability of rolling a total of 7 with two dice is $\dfrac{5}{36}$.

solutions.latex:
A total of 7 comes from $(1,6)$, $(6,1)$, $(2,5)$, $(5,2)$, $(3,4)$ or $(4,3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=2\times\dfrac{x}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{6}\times 2+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}\times 2\\&=\dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}+\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{18}\end{aligned}$$
Setting $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{36}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{5}{36}&=\dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}+\dfrac{5}{36}\\ \dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

$x\ne 0$, as $P(1)$ exists.
$$\therefore x=1$$
$$\therefore P(1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$$

A game involves flipping a coin, then rolling two six-sided dice. If the coin lands heads, the sum of the dice is recorded. If the coin lands tails, the difference between the dice is recorded instead.

When the coin lands heads, a win needs a sum less than $4$, which occurs in $3$ of the $36$ outcomes, so $P(\text{win}\mid H)=\dfrac{3}{36}$.

Heads and tails are equally likely:

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{win}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{30}{36}\right)+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{36}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{11}{24} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(H\mid 4) &= \dfrac{P(H\cap 4)}{P(4)} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{36}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{7} \end{aligned}$$

A credit card requires a six-figure personal identification number (PIN) for purchases. The figures are chosen from the digits $0,1,2,3,\ldots,9$.

Repetition is allowed and the PIN can start with any of the 10 digits.

The credit card is lost and the finder tries to guess the PIN by entering six digits.

parts.latex: What is the probability that the six digits entered are the correct PIN?

Multistage events and tree diagrams.evidence: Each of the six digits is correct with probability 1/10: (1/10)^6

Multiplication principle.reason: Counting 10^6 PINs is an alternative to the solution's method.

parts.latex: What is the probability that the finder will guess at least one digit in its correct position?

solutions.latex:
Each of the six digits is correct with probability $\dfrac{1}{10}$:
$$P(\text{all six correct})=\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)^6=\dfrac{1}{10^6}$$

'At least one correct' is the complement of 'none correct', and each digit is wrong with probability $\dfrac{9}{10}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one correct})&=1-P(\text{none correct})\\&=1-\left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right)^6\\&=0.468559\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A bag contains 4 blue coloured marbles and 6 red coloured marbles. Three marbles are selected at random without replacement.

What is the probability that at least one of the marbles selected is blue?

solutions.latex:
'At least one blue' is the complement of 'no blue':
$$P(\text{no blue})=\dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac{5}{9}\times\dfrac{4}{8}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
$$P(\text{at least one blue})=1-\dfrac{1}{6}=\dfrac{5}{6}$$

parts.latex:
Olivia and Sarah are participating in a fitness program. The probability that Olivia will complete the program is $0.8$, and the probability that Sarah will complete the program is $0.7$.

What is the probability that only one of them will complete the program?

Multistage events and tree diagrams.reason: Multiplying along two paths and adding them.

Complementary events.reason: Needs P(not complete)=1−P(complete) for each person.

Independent events.reason: Events not stated independent; multiply-and-add along paths is Multistage events.

Addition rule and mutually exclusive eve.reason: not_when: adding end-branch probabilities is part of Multistage events.

solutions.latex:
Either Olivia completes and Sarah does not, or Sarah completes and Olivia does not:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{only one})&=0.8\times0.3+0.2\times0.7 \\ &=0.24+0.14 \\ &=0.38 \end{aligned}$$

1701.stem: $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.2$ and $P(A|B)=0.5$

parts.latex: Show that $P(A\cup B)=0.4$.

Find the value of

$$P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)$$

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.2} \\ P(A\cap B)&=0.1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=0.3+0.2-0.1 \\ &=0.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)&=1-P(A\cup B) \\ &=0.6 \end{aligned}$$

1703.stem:
There are 4 red and 3 black discs in a bag. Ms Kim and Ms Lee are playing a game in which they take turns drawing a disc from the bag and then replacing it.

To win the game, Ms Kim must draw a red disc and for Ms Lee to win, she must draw a black disc. They continue taking turns until there is a winner. Ms Kim draws a disc first.

figures.cap: solution sketch: tree diagram of Kim and Lee draws over five turns, red 4/7 and black 3/7
solution sketch: tree diagram continuing turns 5 to 7 (Kim, Lee, Kim)

parts.latex: Find the probability that Ms Kim wins on her first draw.
Find the probability that Ms Kim wins in three or less of her turns.
Find the probability that Ms Kim wins the game.

Applications of arithmetic and geometric.evidence: This is a GP with a=4/7 and r=3/7 x 4/7

solutions.latex: Ms Kim wins on her first draw if she draws a red disc, so $P=\dfrac{4}{7}$.

criteria: Correct expression for the three winning sequences, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{373_q17_s2}

Ms Kim wins by drawing red ($\dfrac{4}{7}$); each earlier round has her draw black ($\dfrac{3}{7}$) and Ms Lee draw red ($\dfrac{4}{7}$):
$$\begin{aligned} P(1 \text{ turn})&=\dfrac{4}{7} \\ P(2 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2 \\ P(3 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^3 \\ P(4 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^3\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^4 \end{aligned}$$
So for $n$ turns,
$$P(n \text{ turns or less})=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^n$$
This is a GP with $a=\dfrac{4}{7}$ and $r=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$. The probability that Ms Kim wins the game is its limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{4}{7}}{1-\frac{3}{7}\times\frac{4}{7}} \\ &=\dfrac{28}{37} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct limiting sum expression, or equivalent merit
Identifies a GP with $r=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$, or equivalent merit

1872.stem:
The probability that Darcy wants to play with a football outside on any particular day is $P(F)$. The probability that it rains on any particular day is $P(R)$.

It is given that $P(F)=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $P(F\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(F'\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

parts.latex: Is Darcy wanting to play with a football outside independent from whether or not it is raining? Justify your answer.
Given that these probabilities stay the same every day, how many days would it take to ensure a 98% chance of Darcy wanting to play football at least once?

solutions.latex:
From the given values, $P(F)=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $P(F')=\dfrac{1}{3}$, $P(F\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(F'\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

\exfigure{388_q15_s1}

Find $P(F\cap R)$ and $P(R)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(F\cap R)&=P(F)-P(F\cap R') \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(R')&=P(F\cap R')+P(F'\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4} \\ P(R)&=1-\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Events are independent if $P(F\cap R)=P(F)\times P(R)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{6}=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Darcy wanting to play football outside is independent of the weather.
criteria: Calculates the additional probabilities, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source also gave a second 'check', $P(F\cup R)=P(F)+P(R)-P(F\cap R)$ ($\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}$). That identity holds for any two events, so it does not test independence; removed. The independence test $P(F\cap R)=P(F)P(R)$ is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
The days are independent, so the chance of no football on any of $n$ days is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n$. Require at least one football day with probability $0.98$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n&=0.98 \\ \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n&=0.02 \\ n&=\dfrac{\log 0.02}{\log\frac{1}{3}} &&(\text{take logs}) \\ &=3.56\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number of days and the chance must be at least $98\%$, so round up.
$$\therefore\ n=4\text{ days}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $1-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n=0.98$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Sums of 8 on the table: $(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)$, which is 5 of the 36 equally likely outcomes.
$$P(\text{score }8)=\dfrac{5}{36}$$

meta.format_note: Marking criteria written by us (the source gave none).

solutions.latex:
The two throws are independent.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both score }8) &= \dfrac{5}{36}\cdot\dfrac{5}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{1296} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Marking criteria written by us (the source gave none).

solutions.latex:
The table is symmetric about the sum 7, so $P(2)=P(12)$, $P(3)=P(11)$, and so on. The sums $2$ to $6$ each have a matching sum from $12$ down to $8$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same}) &= 2\left[P(2\ \&\ 2)+P(3\ \&\ 3)+P(4\ \&\ 4)+P(5\ \&\ 5)+P(6\ \&\ 6)\right]+P(7\ \&\ 7) \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{1^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{2^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{3^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{4^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{5^2}{36^2}\right]+\dfrac{6^2}{36^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2(55)+36}{1296} \\ &= \dfrac{146}{1296} \\ &= \dfrac{73}{648} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $P(\text{same})$ as a sum of the products $P(s)\cdot P(s)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Marking criteria written by us (the source gave none).

solutions.latex:
Barbie's score is greater than, less than, or equal to Ken's, so these probabilities sum to 1.
$$P(B>K)+P(K>B)+P(B=K)=1$$
The game is fair, so $P(B>K)=P(K>B)$ and $P(B=K)=\dfrac{73}{648}$ from part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} 2P(B>K)+\dfrac{73}{648} &= 1 \\ 2P(B>K) &= \dfrac{575}{648} \\ P(B>K) &= \dfrac{575}{1296} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $P(B>K)=P(K>B)$ with the sum of probabilities equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

In a bag of $n$ coloured discs, exactly 7 are red.

The probability that both discs are red is

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{42}{n(n-1)} &= \dfrac{21}{55} \\ \dfrac{2}{n(n-1)} &= \dfrac{1}{55} \\ n(n-1) &= 110 \\ n^2-n-110 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(A\mid B)\times P(B) \\ &=\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{1}{5} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$

Using $P(A'\cap B)=P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ with $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{1}{8}$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} P(A'\cap B)&=\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{40} \end{aligned}$$

If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $P(A)=P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{5}{8}$.

Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=\dfrac{5}{8}+\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{10} \end{aligned}$$

The probability that a person chosen at random has green eyes is $0.04$

Two people are chosen at random.
What is the probability that at least ONE person has green eyes?
What is the smallest number of people that can be chosen at random so that the probability that at least ONE has green eyes is greater than $0.4$?

solutions.latex:
"At least one" is the complement of "none". Each person fails to have green eyes with probability $0.96$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one})&=1-P(\text{none})\\ &=1-0.96\times0.96\\ &=0.0784\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the complementary event, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $n$ people, $P(\text{at least one})=1-(0.96)^n$.
$$\begin{aligned}1-(0.96)^n&>0.4\\ (0.96)^n&<0.6\end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms. Since $\ln0.96<0$, the inequality reverses when dividing.
$$\begin{aligned}n\ln0.96&<\ln0.6\\ n&>\dfrac{\ln0.6}{\ln0.96}=12.51\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n=13 \text{ people}$$

parts.latex: There are 10 green marbles and $W$ white marbles in a bag. The probability of selecting a white marble is $\dfrac{4}{9}$. How many more white marbles need to be added to the bag so that the probability of selecting a white marble from the bag is $\dfrac{3}{5}$?

solutions.latex:
With $W$ white marbles and 10 green marbles, $P(\text{white})=\dfrac{W}{10+W}=\dfrac{4}{9}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9W &= 40+4W \\ 5W &= 40 \\ W &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
So there are 10 green and 8 white marbles. Let $n$ white marbles be added.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{8+n}{18+n} &= \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 40+5n &= 54+3n \\ 2n &= 14 \\ n &= 7 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

A bag contains 4 maroon coloured marbles and 6 white coloured marbles. Three marbles are selected at random without replacement.

What is the probability that at least one of the marbles selected is maroon?

solutions.latex:
Use the complement: at least one maroon marble is the opposite of no maroon marbles.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one maroon})&=1-P(\text{no maroon}) \\ &=1-\left(\dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac{5}{9}\times\dfrac{4}{8}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

3050.stem: Greg lives in Gosford and is starting a new job in Sydney. He needs to catch a train to get to work and will be late if the trains do not run to schedule. The probability that, on any given day, his train will run to schedule is 0.96.

parts.latex: What is the probability that Greg's train is late on the first day?
What is the probability that Greg arrives late on exactly one of the first three days of his new job?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Greg is late})&=1-0.96\\ &=0.04\end{aligned}$$

Exactly one late day can happen in 3 ways (late on day 1, 2 or 3), each with probability $0.04\times0.96^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{late on exactly one day})&=0.04\times0.96^2+0.96\times0.04\times0.96+0.96^2\times0.04\\ &\approx 0.11\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working, or equivalent merit
